title: Bluehaven Logistics — Deployment Criteria Kickoff
next_steps: Redwood: send benchmark template + sample scripts by 2027-06-05
Customer: share representative 1-week traffic traces and payload distributions by 2027-06-07
Schedule on-prem network walkthrough with infra team w/c 2027-06-14
Redwood: provide SOC2 + architecture security matrix link
action_items: Maya Chen: upload benchmark spreadsheet and sample curl scripts — due 2027-06-05
Andre Patel: draft benchmark runbook (latency/throughput/95/99 p99) — due 2027-06-06
Lena Ortiz: export 7-day traffic profile and token distribution — due 2027-06-07

summary: Initial POC scoping to decide Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for realtime inference in logistics routing. Main concerns: 99th percentile latency under 150ms for short queries, cost per 1M tokens, data residency and KMS for PII, and timeline for a 6-week pilot including benchmarks.
questions: What is your target p99 latency and throughput during peak?
Who will be the approval owner for production rollouts?
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-03
Start time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Andre Patel (Redwood SE), Sofia Alvarez (CSM), Jon Park (SE), Sanjay Rao (Bluehaven Head of ML), Lena Ortiz (Infra), Tom Hsu (CTO), Mei Lin (Security), Evan Brooks (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me okay?
[00:07] Sanjay Rao: Yep, loud and clear. Sorry for the slight delay, we had a meeting overrun.
[00:11] Maya Chen: No worries, we wanted to use this time to align on POC success criteria and then dig into hosting options — hosted API vs dedicated capacity vs private deployment. Andre will run through the benchmark plan.
[00:24] Andre Patel: Hey all — quick outline, we'll cover goals, workload sizing, proposed benchmarks (latency, p95/p99, throughput), and then decision criteria for each deployment mode.
[00:33] Tom Hsu: Great. For context our app is an inference microservice for route optimization. Typical request is small, average 120 tokens, peak 200 requests/sec for a region. We need p99 below 150ms for the short queries — otherwise the product experience degrades.
[00:48] Lena Ortiz: And A note on infra: we have VPCs in AWS us-east-1 and a private datacenter for sensitive data. We'll need to understand network egress and whether we can do VPC peering for private mode.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Helpful. Sanjay, can you confirm expected token burn per month at 200 req/s?
[01:11] Sanjay Rao: Rough calc — 200 rps * 86400s * 30 days ~ 518M requests. At 120 tokens average that's ~62B tokens, but that's before caching — we expect a lot of repeated prefixes so effective token count maybe 20-30B.
[01:28] Andre Patel: Okay that's huge and changes recommendations: hosted is great for quick time-to-value, dedicated makes sense for predictable unit costs at that scale, private for residency/compliance. We'll need to do a burn-rate benchmark to validate.
[01:42] Mei Lin: Security question: any PII in payloads? The routing metadata sometimes includes customer IDs and addresses. We need KMS integration and audit logs for every inference call.
[01:53] Maya Chen: Redwood supports KMS integrations and can surface audit logs. For Private deployment we can support customer-managed KMS / HSM. For Hosted, we offer tenant-level encryption and SOC 2 attestation — but for HSM you'd need Dedicated or Private.
[02:09] Evan Brooks: And latency wise, is there a difference between hosted and dedicated?
[02:14] Andre Patel: Short answer — Dedicated usually gives lower and more consistent p99 because you're not contending with multitenant noisy neighbors; Hosted often has good median latency but p99s can vary unless you buy higher tiers or reserved capacity. Our Dedicated pools also give KV cache locality and tuned batching for throughput.
[02:30] Tom Hsu: Can you explain KV cache? We saw it in the docs but not entirely sure how it maps to our workload.
[02:37] Andre Patel: Sure — KV cache stores prefix key-values for commonly requested sequences, so repeated tokens don't re-compute attention. For short repeated prompts, it reduces token compute and also latency. In crowded hosted nodes cache hit rates are lower; in Dedicated/Private you can pin models and warm caches more effectively.
[02:54] Sanjay Rao: That aligns with our use case — we do lots of repeated origin-destination queries with small variations. Cache hit rate could be high.
[03:02] Maya Chen: For the benchmark plan: Andre will send a runbook and sample scripts. We recommend the following tests: 1) p95/p99 latency under steady-state at target RPS, 2) tail latency under burst (2x peak), 3) throughput with batching and without batching, 4) cost-per-1M tokens estimate.
[03:20] Andre Patel: We'll include agent-based and remote curl scripts to measure end-to-end latency. Also we'll instrument tracing and token-level timing to see where time is spent (network vs model decode).
[03:32] Lena Ortiz: Network — we need to know egress patterns. For Private/on-prem we don't want traffic leaving our VPC. Can Private be fully air-gapped?
[03:41] Jon Park: Redwood Private can be deployed air-gapped or with a customer-controlled control plane. There are variants — full on-prem package vs VPC-connected private. We'll put the options in the security matrix.
[03:53] Mei Lin: Does Redwood keep any data in hosted? What about logs and retention?
[03:57] Sofia Alvarez: We can set log retention policies and ensure PII redaction. For hosted we do process data transiently and support customer requests for data deletion; for Private you control retention. We'll share the SOC2 + data handling doc.
[04:09] Sanjay Rao: Back to cost — at 20-30B tokens monthly, we need per-token cost clarity. Hosted tier pricing is straightforward but might be expensive at that volume; Dedicated is committed capacity. Private has licensing and infra cost overhead.
[04:23] Andre Patel: We'll run cost modeling in the benchmark spreadsheet — factoring reserved GPU hours, QPS, batching gains, and KV cache hit. In many cases, Dedicated ends up lower TCO for sustained high volume.
[04:34] Tom Hsu: Timeline: we want pilot acceptance in 6 weeks if possible. Week 1: data/traces + runbook. Week 2–3: benchmark runs. Week 4: evaluate results and security review. Week 5–6: small canary in prod or staging. Does that match Redwood's typical pilot?
[04:49] Maya Chen: Yes, that's a reasonable cadence. We usually do a 4–8 week pilot with benchmarks in first 2–3 weeks. We'll align the SLOs and acceptance criteria up front.
[04:58] Evan Brooks: On the SLOs, our acceptance criteria: p99 <= 150ms, median < 60ms, accuracy/regression within 1% of baseline outputs, and cost target of <$X per 1M tokens (we'll provide exact number).
[05:12] Andre Patel: Noted. For accuracy/regression we recommend running a prompt set and diff outputs across model variants — Redwood has eval harness but customer needs to supply a gold set.
[05:23] Sanjay Rao: We'll provide a seed eval set of 2k prompts.
[05:27] Maya Chen: Great. Any red flags or blockers we should be aware of?
[05:30] Lena Ortiz: Network egress approvals might take 2 weeks — if hosted option requires cross-account peering or firewall changes, that could delay.
[05:39] Mei Lin: Also legal needs to review DPA and data flow for hosted. If we require HSM + on-prem keys, that pushes towards Dedicated/Private.
[05:48] Tom Hsu: Are there hybrid options? Like run core model in Private for sensitive tokens and use Hosted for non-sensitive?
[05:56] Andre Patel: Yes — smart routing supports policy-based splits. You can route sensitive requests to Private/Dedicated and non-sensitive to Hosted; Redwood can do fallbacks and A/Bing. We'll capture routing rules in the design doc.
[06:08] Sanjay Rao: How do you measure cache hit rate?
[06:10] Andre Patel: We'll instrument hit/miss counters and provide dashboards. During benchmark we'll run synthetic repeats to estimate realistic hit rates.
[06:17] [00:06:20] Customer (overlap): ok sorry interuption —
[06:21] Maya Chen: No problem — rough mid-call crosstalk. Back to activation: for Dedicated, what GPU family are we considering? A100? H100?
[06:30] Andre Patel: For this workload, H100 gives better latency at lower batch sizes but is more expensive. A100 or L40S variants can be good too depending on quantization and model. We'll recommend based on benchmark results.
[06:44] Lena Ortiz: Do you support int8/4 quantization for our models?
[06:47] Andre Patel: Yes, Redwood supports quantized execution and we have quantization profiles. But quality checks are critical — we'll run evals pre/post quantization.
[06:55] Tom Hsu: Ok timeline and owners — can we recap?
[06:58] Maya Chen: Sure: Redwood sends benchmark scripts and spreadsheet (Maya/Andre), Bluehaven shares traffic traces+payloads (Lena/Sanjay), Security list of KMS/HSM and residency constraints (Mei), run benchmarks w/c 2027-06-14, review results w/c 2027-06-21.
[07:13] Sanjay Rao: Sounds good. Two nitty-gritty items: 1) our product expects sub-200ms round-trip including network hop to client; we need to include edge latency in tests. 2) We have a legal hold on some datasets — will need to map data flows.
[07:28] Maya Chen: We'll include end-to-end agent tests from your edge nodes. For legal hold, we'll coordinate with the compliance team and provide a data flow diagram.
[07:36] [00:07:37] Andre Patel: Quick technical deep-dive — sample benchmark plan details: cold-start latency, steady-state with warmed KV cache, bursty traffic with 2x surge. We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and CPU/GPU utilization.
[07:50] Jon Park: Also instrument queueing delay and batching stats so we can tune batch windows. For low-latency workloads, we often recommend continuous batching with small windows to keep p99 low.
[08:00] Lena Ortiz: We're worried about throttling — if you autoscale, how long to scale up?
[08:05] Andre Patel: Dedicated pools can be sized for headroom; autoscale delta is minutes depending on the infra. For Hosted we can burst to higher tiers but that may increase p99 temporarily. We'll show examples from similar customers.
[08:18] Tom Hsu: Any compliance concerns with embeddings? We plan to store embeddings in our own DB.
[08:23] Sofia Alvarez: If you store embeddings yourself, that's fine — Redwood can return embeddings and not retain them. We'll include the embedding retention policy in the security doc.
[08:31] Sanjay Rao: One more: if we go Dedicated, can we pin a specific model family and fallback to open models?
[08:36] Andre Patel: Yes, pinning and fallback policies are supported. You can do canary rollouts to test newer versions.
[08:42] [00:08:43] random background noise then resume
[08:48] Mei Lin: For Private, the ops burden on our team is a concern. How much support does Redwood provide for on-prem deployments?
[08:56] Maya Chen: We offer an on-site deployment package and runbook; for Private there's a licensing + support SLA. Typically we embed a deployment engineer for the first 2–4 weeks. We'll include that in the commercial term sheet.
[09:08] Evan Brooks: Do you have references in logistics or similar throughput customers?
[09:12] Maya Chen: Yes — we can share anonymized case studies. Will follow up with 2 references who have done Dedicated pilots.
[09:19] Tom Hsu: Ok, last question — if benchmarks show we can't hit p99 target on Hosted, do you help with migration path?
[09:26] Andre Patel: Absolutely, we'll map migration steps: test on Dedicated, tune batching/quantization, and then plan cutover with traffic-shifting and rollback policies.
[09:35] Maya Chen: Alright, let's summarize concrete next steps — Andre, you'll share the runbook and scripts by Friday 2027-06-05. Bluehaven will share traces and eval set by Monday 2027-06-07. We'll reconvene after initial benchmark runs.
[09:48] Sanjay Rao: Confirmed. Appreciate the clarity.
[09:51] Maya Chen: Great — any other open items?
[09:54] Lena Ortiz: Please add network engineering to the invite for the walkthrough.
[09:58] Maya Chen: Will do. Sofia will coordinate.
[10:02] Sofia Alvarez: I'll send a calendar invite for the network walkthrough and include the redwood security doc.
[10:08] Tom Hsu: Thanks everyone.
[10:10] Maya Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with the docs.
[10:14] [End of recording]

Notes on transcription: there are a few mis-heard words (K V cache was sometimes transcribed as K V cash), speaker labels may be approximated, and timestamps are approximate.
